ARTICLE IN PRESS The Aesthetics of Comparativeness in Clifford Geertz's Islam Observed Abstract Interdisciplinarity and comparativeness in studying complex phenomena, such as religion, proved to be of very crucial utility either as methodology or as analytical model. In Islam Observed: S Religious Development in Morocco and Indonesia, theS anthropologist Clifford Geertz E demonstrated the extent to which cultural anthropology can recount and revisit social formulations R of religions and thus reopen new horizons and positionalities in understanding and perceiving P religion practices by employing a comparative methodology that combines disciplines of N anthropology, ethnography, sociology, and literature. Geertz’s comparative perspective in tracing I the foundational formation of Islam in two distinct geographical contexts (i.e. Indonesia and E Morocco) is notably significant. ThLis article seeks to explore the comparative concepts he C employed, particularly the notion of aesthetic codes, which illuminate the diverse practices of I T Islam across regions. It also highlights the role of cultural poetics in shaping the belief systems of R societies situated in geographically distant parts of the Islamic world. It also engages critically A with the literary aura in Geertz’s comparative approach by extending the reflection with more recent theories in comparative and world literature. Keywords Comparativeness. Aesthetics. Cultural anthropology. Islam Observed. Clifford Geertz. 1 ARTICLE IN PRESS 1. Introduction Clifford Geertz developed a significant aesthetic methodology in his prominent publication about Islam in Indonesia and Morocco entitled ‘Islam Observed; Religious Development in Morocco and Indonesia’ (1968). The study instituted on two modes of analysis: the first consists of studying the symbols of Indonesian and Moroccan culture, and their performances while interacting with religion as witnessed and observed in two geographical spaces: island of Java in Indonesia and city of Sefrou in North Morocco. The second analytical model, on the other hand, stands on historical accounts that he utilized to understand the shifts in traditional practices of Islam. Geertz codified each country’s cultural poetics by using the aesthetics of comparativeness and thus S creating paralleled streams of culture identities. As such, Geertz stated that civilization in Morocco S was built on ‘nerve’ in contrast with Indonesia’s religion that is established on ‘diligence’ (Geertz E 1968). He maintained that Islam came to Indonesia byR sea: not on the heels of conquest but by P trade, and is characterized by its inwardness, imperturbability, patience, poise, sensibility, aestheticism, elitism, and radical disillusionmNent of individuality (Geertz 1968). Conversely, I Morocco’s Islam, he argued, is built on activism, fervor, impetuosity, nerve, toughness, moralism, E populism, and an almost obsessive self-assertion. The force of religion – said Geertz- is stronger L in Morocco than Indonesia, but itsC scope is less encompassing. In Morocco, religion only affects I few parts of life, but it is felt intensely (Geertz 1968). These dichotomies demonstrate how local T cultures and social ethics fRunction as crucial determinants in the construction of nationally-abound A religions by adjusting spirituality with cultural awareness of societies. Previous research reacted against Geertz’ approach in different ways. Asad Taha (1993), for instance, criticized the Western and Christian influence on Geertz’ perspective of Islam, claiming that Geertz did not take into account other historical and cultural attributes. Similarly, both Bagader (1993) and Bowen (1993) highlighted Geertz’ heavy reliance on the Western representations about Islam and the limitation of the so-called ‘symbolic anthropology’ in understanding different practices of everyday Islam, which implicates local perceptions of Islam against the odds of nationalist ideology of the state. Lindholm, C. (2002) and Varisco, D. M. (2005) focused on the generalization of Geertz’ approach, while Iggers, G. G. (2005) pointed on Geertz’s interpretive-based insights. Others, such as Kaptein, N. J. G. (2018) and Rani, Z (2018), counted numerous limitations of Geertz’ theory including the absence of historical development of Islam 2 ARTICLE IN PRESS in both countries, the role of political Islam, gender, and violence among other issues in formulation the modern Islam. Therefore, each study portrays Clifford Geertz as an outsider coming from completely a different humanistic tradition, someone who does not monitor the complexity of religion in the dedicated countries and thereby neglecting the significant foundational attributes of Islam in the countries under study. However, the importance of Clifford Geertz’ study, as I argue it, rests in the non-traditional analytical tools he used to understand the socio-cultural attributes that determine the practices of Islam in these two distinct societies. In this sense, this article investigates the way Clifford Geertz used what might be called ‘comparative aesthetic codes’ by tracing the cultural symbols and their artistic and poetic significance against what Geertz called ‘common sense’. The analysis also charts the way religion and religious S institutions function as a ‘social history of the imagination’ through which societies perceive and S practice their beliefs. E R P 2. The Aesthetic Codes in Geertz’ Comparative Analysis N I E Clifford Geertz’ writing is characterized by its literary-oriented shape, portraying anthropology L through such literary terminologyC as rhetoric, metaphoric, and symbolic. This writing strategy I highlights afresh the critiques and debates regarding the relationship between literary studies, T R anthropology, and ethnography, which are the connections that culminated into the so-called A ‘literary Anthropology’ (Geertz 1988 & Rapport 1994), the type of anthropology that gives significant credits to storytelling and text crafting. The literary underpinnings of Geertz’ anthropological writings were derived from two academic convictions: first, he considered anthropology as textual construction evaluated and developed in conjunction between various types of cultural systems. Second, he attempted ‘to steer anthropological scholarship away from a rigidly scientific model and toward a humanistic, interpretive, hermeneutic model-apparently with great success’(Olson 1991, 245). Geerts’ intended to transcend the narrow disciplinary hindrances and reach an open interdisciplinary vision by formulating a pluralistic view that comprises literature, aesthetics, and other fields of humanities. As such, Geertz was deeply concerned with questions of language and discourse, not from the merely linguistic perspective, important as it is, but from his conviction that linguistic discourses have significance in cultural anthropology and 3 ARTICLE IN PRESS humanistic discoveries. Equally noticeable is his consideration of the social sciences not as abstract facts or scientifically based fields, but as ‘fiction’ where ‘meaning is socially, historically, and rhetorically constructed’(Olson 1991, 246). In this sense, Geertz’s anthropological insights produced a kind of humanistic “second text,” composed of key symbolic concepts that serve both representative and referential functions. These concepts collectively form what might be described as aesthetic codes – structures that echo and embody rich aesthetic and poetic knowledge, offering a comparative lens through which to understand the humanistic dimensions of Islam as constructed and expressed across diverse and distant societies. These aesthetic codes are rhetorically connotative, intellectually recognizable, and S culturally referable. They emerge from the accumulated sociocultural histories of religious S practice, which Geertz systematically codified into symbolicE frameworks. These symbolic systems R possess a regressive yet compelling quality: they invite readers to trace the ethnological P cartography of meaning, revealing how these conc epts evolve through historical layering within N specific cultural contexts. I Geertz makes a comparison betwee n the cultural foundations of Islam in Morocco and E Indonesia, contesting that the first is Lbuilt on ‘nerve’, ‘conquest’ and Arabic tradition, while the C latter stands on ‘diligence’, and Indic tradition. For Geertz, Indonesian Islam came by the ‘sea’ I and ‘trade’ while the Islam ofT Morocco arrived by ‘war’ and ‘conquest’ (Geertz 1968). As noticed, R every representative concept directs the audience’s attention to its historical formation as a A condition to understand the very correspondence of these concepts with the fact they conceptualize. To critically engage with the concept of the ‘Islam of the sea,’ which is characterized by diligence, inwardness, imperturbability, patience, poise, sensibility, aestheticism, and elitism, it is essential to examine the historical conditions underpinning its emergence in Indonesia, alongside the sociocultural mechanisms through which these values are articulated and sustained within an organized cultural framework. In fact, the very focus of modern anthropology of culture – with Clifford Geertz as one of its pioneering scholars – is the ‘socially available systems of significance’ (Geertz 1968, 95) whereby societies create and adopt a body of values, languages, ethics, and norms in a form of social system through which meaning is engendered. However, cultural anthropology identifies the ‘system’ not only as an organized institutional hierarchy such as the Mosque, the Zawiya, and 4 ARTICLE IN PRESS the Quranic School, but also as the hidden sequence of social relations embedded in the daily social practices where values and perceptions have pragmatic importance. In Islam Observed, Clifford Geertz codifies the meta-relations and social practices that have been historically accumulated through the prolonged processes of integration and domestication of Islamic doctrine. Geertz employs two emblematic figures as metaphoric representations to illustrate the establishment and evolution of Islamic tradition within distinct cultural milieus. The Indonesian exemplar, Sunan Kalidjaga, is portrayed as a pivotal agent in the Islamization of Indonesia. Paradoxically, his engagement with Islam unfolds without direct reference to the Qur'an; instead, his religiosity is shaped by a form of enlightenment grounded in detached stoicism (Geertz 1968, 28). In contrast, the Moroccan figure, Lyusi (1691), is depicted S as a prominent religious and spiritual authority endowed with baraka – a form of divine charisma S – which legitimizes his status as a Sherif, a descendant ofE the Prophet, thereby entitling him to R specific honours, privileges, and reverence (Geertz 1968, 35). P Indeed, these two figures have played pivot al roles in establishing what Geertz recognized N as an ‘Indonesian Islam’, which is explicitly different from the Moroccan Islam. Geertz’ I comparative method relies, it should be note d, on the poetic and aesthetic connotations of the codes E he utilized as analytical tools to makeL sense of the religious practices in Indonesia and Morocco. C Accordingly, Geertz drew upon the methodologies of area studies to trace the historical and I intellectual formation of the Ttwo principal figures: Kalidjaga, depicted as ‘immobile’, and Lyusi, R who ‘travelled relentlessly’. This contrast underscores the role of value circulation and A transnational mobility in shaping the intellectual trajectories and cultural embeddedness of these emblematic individuals. That being said, Geertz does not sufficiently situate these two figures within the political contexts of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries in Indonesia and Morocco; contexts that profoundly shaped the production of Islamic thought during that period. On one hand, Morocco’s political structure was rooted in an authoritarian monarchy fostered by Islamic traditionalism. On the other hand, Indonesia’s political landscape evolved into a revolutionary and pluralistic system, later characterized by Sukarno’s model of Guided Democracy The two concepts represent alternatively two different characters depicting a very personalized religious logic whereby ‘encounter’ and ‘immobile’ will demarcate the distinctive features of Islam aesthetics in Morocco and Indonesia. Significantly, the figure of Kalidjaga embodies a mode of religious reception and reproduction in which Islam, originating from distant 5 ARTICLE IN PRESS regions, is internalized without necessitating physical transgression of local boundaries. In contrast, the Moroccan and broader North African context reflects a different trajectory: Islam was initially introduced through conquest and subsequently flourished through the efforts of mobile religious elites who traversed east and west in pursuit of recognized centers of Islamic learning. This emphasis on mobility underscores a valorization of outward movement as a means of accessing wisdom and authentic religious knowledge directly from its foundational sources, a principle deeply embedded in the doctrinal consciousness of North African scholars and believers. This epistemological orientation aligns with the core methodology of Hadith sciences, wherein transmission is governed by rigorous protocols. Narrators adhere to a meticulously structured chain of transmission (isnād), ensuring the integrity and authenticity of the Prophet’s sayings through an S unbroken sequence of reliable transmitters. S The immobility, on the other hand, highlights Ethe status of self-acquaintance, self- R repletion, and the full dependence on inwardness that does not necessitate any external movement P to reach religious truth. As such, the Indonesian Isla m is characterized as an ‘Indic Islam’ in which N the Indian sea is the sole medium of connection with the original Islamic sources. This relative I medium plays another crucial role in constru cting the aesthetics of the Indonesian Islam as opposed E to the Moroccan Islam brought by andL through land. According to Geertz, the space of movement C and connection is significant to cultural anthropology as it provides another dimension of I explanation that serve as a mTaterial key to decipher other sides of the religious practices in two R different geographical spaces. Hence, the two spaces have been used by Geertz to explain and A understand the aesthetics and logic of thinking in Indonesia and Morocco by relocating their religious practices to the very foundational mediums of religious truth. 3. Symbolic Systems and Comparativeness Geertz conceptual analysis embody indeed a problematic epistemic tendency throughout his complete dependence on the theory of symbolic system (Harnad 1992) whereby concepts play connotative and denotative prominence in a coherent system of cultural values. Concepts are considered as being bound, homogenic, coherent, stable, and structural, whereas social reality is characterized by its variability, inconsistencies, conflict, change, and individual agency. For Geertz, concepts do represent an everyday repeated social life, and only in this condition that 6 ARTICLE IN PRESS ‘culture should be retained as a convenient term for designating the clusters of common concepts, emotions, and practices that arise when people interact regularly’ (Brumann 1999, 51). Ultimately, concepts preserve their cultural weight by being contextualized within the cultural framework that gives them holistic meaning. While this conceptual analysis was praised generally by scholars of cultural anthropology, yet Geertz’ insights have been criticized tremendously especially regarding the employment of comparative analysis. For Geertz, the comparative tactic is always present in cultural anthropology where comparison is, by definition, the employment of a method for constructing analytical relations among ideal types, which leads to discovering ‘elective affinities’ (Schmidt 2010, 98). In Islam Observed, Clifford Geertz asks: “Is the comparative study of religion condemned to S mindless description and an equally mindless celebration of the unique?” (Geertz 1968, 54). His S answer was negative because the field of comparative religEion is but an ‘ordered universe whose R order we shall discover precisely by comparing, with some circumstantiality, cases drawn from P different parts of it’ (Geertz 1968, 55). And y et, anthropology continues to grapple with N methodological limitations in its comparative approach, particularly when comparing I ethnographic cases, where challenges arise in defining the case, determining its dimensions, and E accounting for the growing interconnLectedness of the world (Schnegg 2014, 57). One proposed C avenue to overcome such limitations is by combining new comparative agenda that utilizes I multilevel comparison (SchnTegg 2014, 55), and more strictly to draw comparison as to rest on R sound historical reconstructions to understand the processes that lead to similar forms where A culture has developed (Boas 1996, 905). Aware of such limitations, Clifford Geertz advances his comparative methodology by asserting its necessary positionality within the disciplines of cultural anthropology and comparative religion. Central to his theoretical framework is the concept of thick description, which refers to a mode of analysis that attends to the multiplicity of behaviors and social relations within their full contextual complexity, thereby rendering them intelligible to an outsider. This approach does not preclude the use of thin description, which involves a concentrated focus on a single site or localized subject matter to uncover subtle insights that may elude broader analyses (Geertz 1968, 4). Geertz’s thick description resonates with Immanuel Wallerstein’s world-systems analysis (1974), particularly as a postmodernist methodology aimed at tracing the circulation of culture, 7 ARTICLE IN PRESS signs, and objects across diverse and shifting spatial contexts. Nevertheless, both approaches have faced criticism (especially when applied in isolation) for being either overly committed to localism or excessively aligned with global systemic frameworks. Geertz navigates this tension by employing a dynamic methodological lens, zooming in and out to interpret sociocultural practices. In doing so, he demonstrates how small-scale phenomena acquire significance only in relation to larger systemic structures, and vice versa, thereby reinforcing the interdependence of micro and macro analytical perspectives. These debates have sparked the problematics of “Text” within the context of hermeneutics, particularly in relation to literary, anthropological, and religious discourse. Two principal analytical methodologies have emerged in this regard. The first is close reading, which entails a S detailed analysis of texts in and of themselves, without situating them within broader contextual S frameworks. The second is distant reading, a method that iEnterprets texts in relation to expansive R and complex systems of thought, often privileging patterns, circulation, and intertextuality across P wider cultural terrains. N Clifford Geertz articulates a similar distinction in his analysis of the methodological I tensions within ethnography and anthropo logy, referring to “the Written At” and “the Written E About” (Geertz 1988, 144). This distiLnction underscores the epistemological challenges of textual C representation and positionality in fieldwork and cultural interpretation. As I argue, Geertz’s I concepts of thick and thin dTescription draw methodological inspiration from critical debates in R comparative and world literature—particularly those concerning how texts traverse local A boundaries and attain global resonance. His approach implicitly synthesizes both close and distant reading, allowing for a nuanced understanding of how meaning is constructed through layered textual and cultural engagements. Literary critic Franco Moretti criticized the so-called ‘close reading’ in its incarnations, from the new criticism to deconstruction, because it necessarily depends on an extremely ‘small canon’ (Moretti 2013, 48). Anthropology and ethnography similarly build its knowledge on small canons as they focus particularly on the local lives, cultures and beliefs while constructing their analytical models. Moretti argues that distant reading is a ‘condition of knowledge’ because it allows you to focus on units that are much smaller or much larger than the text: devices, themes, tropes, or genres and systems (Moretti 2013, 49). Equally evident are the limitations of world- systems theory, particularly in its tendency to forcibly relocate texts into broader global 8 ARTICLE IN PRESS frameworks even when such positioning conflicts with their cultural origins. As Walter Mignolo notes, global designs do not always govern local linguistic landscapes or epistemological cartographies (Mignolo 2000, 255), although this might be true especially in the era of globalization and open borders. For Geertz, there exist a textual connection between the ‘Being Here’ and ‘Being There’ as a dialectical condition within which anthropology functions by merging the ‘Written At’ and ‘Written About’, which, for him, is the amalgam that gives power to cultural anthropology. The Geertz’s heavy dependency on the symbolic system in interpreting Islam also shows the limitation of this system; it is a system which could not expand its horizon into a more holistic system incorporating Islamic theology with law, gender, political power, and the production of S everyday internal discourses. Incorporating these essential attributes into the analysis challenges S integrated research on Islam that risks essentializing it into Eexoticized cultural binaries. Islam has R never been solely defined by the legal norms of Sharia; rather, it constitutes a plural system P encompassing multiple normative registers, inclu ding philosophy, art, Sufism, and aesthetic N expression (Ahmed,S 2016). It cannot be reduced to broad cultural “born flaws” (Cai 2024), nor I can it be fully captured by Geertz’s thick description, which has been critiqued for relying on E idealized conceptions of culture and Lindividualist presuppositions (Balmaceda 2023). And yet, C recent calls for ‘deep and vertical’ ethnography, emphasizing materiality, silence, affect, the I unsaid, and the gaps (Helin Tet al. 2023), do not fully resolve the limitations inherent in thick R description. As I argue, culture operates within a larger system of complex, interconnected A attributes, none of which can be meaningfully understood in isolation from the broader systemic whole. It should be noted, however, that Geertz’s legacy has shifted extensively the study of Islam as its cultural turn, not only in anthropology but also in connection with other disciplines. In his Islamic Intellectual History in the Seventeenth Century: Scholarly Currents in the Ottoman Empire and the Maghreb (El-Rouayheb 2015), Khaled El-Rouayheb traces comparatively the intellectual history of the Ottoman Empire and the Maghreb during the seventeenth century, a period which, he argues, has escaped the extensive attention in academia. El-Rouayheb’s methodology focuses on the scholarly trends in that period through a close reading of some prominent figures such as Ibrāhīm al-Kūrānī (d. 1690), al-Ḥasan al-Yūsī (d. 1691), ʿAbd al-Ghanī al-Nābulusī (d. 1731), Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb (d. 1792), al-Zabīdī (d. 1791), and al-Shawkānī (d. 1834), just to name a few. 9 ARTICLE IN PRESS The aims of this scholarly cartography were threefold: first, to trace the growing interest in rational sciences, particularly through the widespread use of taḥqīq (verification) in the Ottoman Empire and broader Muslim world; second, to examine the intertextuality and mutual influence among prominent scholars of the period; and third, to argue for the significance of this intellectual flourishing in shaping European humanism and Enlightenment thought. El-Rouayheb’s distinctive contribution lies in his transnational, transcultural, and transdisciplinary approach, which combines both close and distant reading to construct a holistic account of how ideas and theories circulated across the borders of the Ottoman Empire and the Maghreb during the seventeenth century. His research builds upon the scholarly legacy of Geertz by employing a comparative method to trace the emergence and development of Islamic S intellectual history. He positions key intellectual figures as fulcrums through which to examine S how ideas traverse and circulate across diverse geographiEcal regions within the Islamic world. R Notably, the outcomes of El-Rouayheb’s work resonate with Geertz’s intellectual project: both P foreground the role of ‘men of knowledge’: their te xts, their mobility, and the spatial contexts that N shape their intellectual production. While Geertz relies on symbolic systems as analytical tools, I El-Rouayheb focuses on systems of thought as they were distinctly articulated in two major Islamic E regions: the Ottoman Empire and theL Maghreb. This methodological divergence underscores the C continued relevance of Geertz’s approach within Islamic Studies, even as its limitations become I apparent in addressing the fuTll spectrum of foundational religious practices and their historical R underpinnings. Conclusion Widely recognized as a key contributor to both anthropology and the study of Islam, Clifford Geertz’s theory of cultural systems centers on the pivotal role of socio-linguistic structures and symbolic systems in shaping anthropological discourse. His approach is deeply rooted in language, particularly in its capacity to render the actual, to make meaning ‘vitality phrased’ (Geertz 1988, 143). This reliance on language is essential to achieving the ethnographic imperative: to analyze, explain, amuse, disconcert, celebrate, edify, excuse, astonish, and subvert (Geertz 1988, 42). 10 ARTICLE IN PRESS In this framework, language becomes the vehicle through which rhetorical expressions produced by Muslim societies in specific historical and cultural contexts are understood as symbolic systems of knowledge, or what this article refers to as “aesthetic codes.” However, the heavy reliance on rhetorical language as a subjective medium cannot, on its own, fully account for sociological or anthropological phenomena, which are often grounded in objective realities. Nevertheless, it can illuminate dimensions of truth that remain obscured by conventional socio- cultural analysis, particularly when interdisciplinary methods are employed. To this end, Islamic practices across diverse Muslim societies cannot be adequately understood without considering a constellation of factors: geographical space, cultural relations, historical narratives, connections to global centers of Islamic learSning, and the roles of language S and translation. This article acknowledges Geertz’s critical contribution in employing humanistic E methodologies to compare Islam in Indonesia and Morocco through a literary-comparative lens. JSON: Name: aesthetic_codes_pipeline Title: A computational comparative pipeline that operationalizes aesthetic-code linguistic features to classify and explain regional representations of Islam in ethnographic texts Short Hypothesis: Explicitly extracted aesthetic-code linguistic features (metaphor and rhetorical device counts, mobility-token frequencies, named-figure network centrality, and stylistic metrics) cause a statistically significant increase in classification accuracy for distinguishing Morocco-derived versus Indonesia-derived ethnographic accounts compared with baseline topic-model and raw-embedding features. Related Work: Prior approaches divide into qualitative symbolic-anthropology methods emphasizing thick description and literary close reading, and quantitative distant-reading/text-mining methods using topic models, embeddings, and stylometrics. Qualitative methods capture contextualized meaning and rhetorical nuance but lack scalability, reproducibility, and quantitative testability; they also often rely on limited canons and omit political-historical covariates. Quantitative methods scale and enable statistical testing but typically reduce texts to topical or distributional patterns that miss metaphor, mobility narratives, named-figure roles, and other rhetorical-aesthetic devices central to comparative cultural claims. Hybrid studies remain limited: existing hybridizations either use simple bag-of-words augmentations or treat qualitative codes as sparse labels without integrated feature extraction. Unresolved issues include operationalizing aesthetic codes, validating that such features carry regionally discriminative signal beyond topical confounds, and quantifying how close-reading annotations complement distant-reading models. Abstract: This project addresses whether the literary-anthropological notion of aesthetic codes can be operationalized as measurable linguistic features that improve comparative classification and explanation of regional representations of Islam in ethnographic texts. We propose a pipeline that combines manual close-reading annotation of aesthetic codes with automated distant-reading extraction modules: metaphor and rhetorical-device detectors, mobility-token and travel-verb counters, named-figure entity-network metrics, and multi-level stylistic features. We will assemble a labeled corpus of ethnographic chapters and historical accounts focused on Morocco and Indonesia, extract the aesthetic-code feature set, and evaluate their predictive power in supervised classification and explanatory regression tasks against baselines using topic models and raw embeddings. Main contributions are (1) a reproducible feature taxonomy for aesthetic codes, (2) an integrated extraction and modeling pipeline, and (3) empirical evidence quantifying the explanatory and predictive value of aesthetic codes relative to standard text-mining features. Expected outcome: measurable validation of whether aesthetic codes encode region-specific comparative signals and identification of their limits for broader generalization. Experiments: Datasets: create a multilingual corpus of approximately 250-400 documents (ethnographic monograph chapters, published articles, primary historical narratives) labeled by regional origin (Morocco or Indonesia) and annotated for a set of close-reading aesthetic-code labels on a 200-document subset. Metadata fields: year, author, genre, translation status, and known political-historical indicators (e.g., colonial context, mobility indices). Preprocessing: tokenize, lemmatize, sentence-segment, align translations where applicable. Feature sets: (A) baseline_topic: LDA topic proportions (k=50); (B) baseline_embed: pretrained transformer embeddings averaged per doc; (C) stylometry: sentence length, lexical richness, POS distributions; (D) aesthetic_manual: human-annotated binary/ordinal codes for metaphor prevalence, rhetorical framing, named-figure prominence, mobility orientation; (E) aesthetic_auto: automated detectors producing counts/scores for metaphors, rhetorical markers, travel/mobility verbs, named-entity network centralities, and semantic-frame occurrences. Models: train supervised classifiers (logistic regression with L2, random forest, SVM, and fine-tuned transformer classifier) using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. Evaluation metrics: accuracy, macro F1, precision/recall per class, ROC-AUC. Statistical tests: paired bootstrap and permutation tests for significance of performance differences. Ablations: (1) full feature set vs without aesthetic_auto; (2) aesthetic_auto alone vs baseline_embed; (3) aesthetic_manual + aesthetic_auto vs baseline_topic; (4) remove mobility features; (5) domain transfer: train on Indonesia documents test on Morocco and vice versa. Explanatory analyses: logistic regression coefficients and SHAP values to identify feature importance; regressions of aesthetic features on external metadata (mobility index, political centralization) evaluated with adjusted R-squared and significance. Clustering: run hierarchical and k-means clustering on combined features and evaluate adjusted rand index relative to region labels. Replication: provide data splits and code to reproduce all experiments. Risk Factors and Limitations: Annotation subjectivity and inter-annotator variability in defining aesthetic codes; translation artefacts biasing lexical and rhetorical signals across languages; corpus size limitations leading to overfitting, especially for deep models; spurious correlations between topical content and region labels confounding attribution to aesthetic codes; limited ability of automated detectors to reliably identify metaphors and rhetorical devices across historical registers; reductionism risk when quantifying nuanced qualitative phenomena; inability to capture political, gender, or institutional contexts not present in texts, limiting causal generalization; ethical risks of reifying cultural stereotypes if automated outputs are interpreted without qualitative checks; compute costs for fine-tuning transformer models and running permutation tests for large numbers of features; constrained external validity beyond the assembled corpus and historical periods represented.
